It pervades all three realms;
the mind of retribution is not fixed.
According to the *Vibhāṣā*:
There are two explanations.
One school proclaims that from the third dhyāna downward,
there is no retribution for the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
If this principle holds,
then from the third dhyāna downward, there is no one who passes away with a mind of retribution;
one must necessarily pass away with a mind of equanimity.
Therefore, according to one school's teaching,
there is also the abandonment of retribution from the third dhyāna downward.
If this interpretation is followed:
The death-moment consciousness of retribution is pervasive throughout the three realms; within these,
one dies from either the middle or the lower [levels].
Regarding those who are reborn in higher realms:
they must die within one of the three types of minds—those acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika*), those born of retribution (*vipākaja*), or those of deportment (*airyāpathika*).
This is because if there were unwholesome or defiled states of a lower level, one would not be reborn in a higher realm.
If one dies in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and is reborn in a lower realm,
one necessarily dies in a mind acquired at birth (*upapattipratilambhika*), a defiled mind of retribution (*vipākaja*),
or a mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*), because there is no unwholesome mind in any of the higher stages.
If one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in a lower realm,
they must die within one of the three types of minds acquired at birth— namely, those that produce defiled retribution—
because they lack unwholesome minds of deportment.
If one dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the desire realm,
one may pass away while in any of the five types of minds.
If one dies in the form realm and is reborn in that same stage,
four types of consciousness terminate at death,
excluding the unwholesome consciousness.
Regarding the meaning of whether or not there is retribution-consciousness from the third dhyāna downward,
it has been adjudicated as above.
For now, we shall discuss the case where it exists.
If one dies in the formless realm and is to be reborn in that same place,
they must pass away from three types of minds— those acquired at birth, those that are defiled, or those born of retribution.
This is because such a being lacks unwholesome minds or minds of deportment.

Question: Why is it that the mind of skillful means, the mind of those in training (śaikṣa), the mind of those beyond training (aśaikṣa), and the mind of craftsmanship or transformation cannot bring about death?
Answer: Because at the time of death, the mind is weak and inferior.
One must not die with such a forced mind;
such is the nature of birth and death.
Next, the sequence of the arising of various mental states will be distinguished.
Within this context, the sequence is clarified solely by means of immediate succession in arising.
There are seven such sequences.
First, the sequence of the arising of phenomena that coexist:
this refers to how phenomena belonging to the same level arise as mutual causes for one another.
Second, the sequence of the cultivation and arising of higher phenomena.
For example, based on desire, one initiates the first dhyāna and so forth; thirdly,
there is the sequence of preventing faults regarding lower states,

such as when, based on the wholesome mind of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of a higher level or a defiled mind, one gives rise to the innate wholesome states (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) of a lower level.
Fourth, the sequence of retrogression from lower dharmas,
such as when one relies on superior wholesome states and retrogresses to give rise to lower fetters.
Fifth, the sequence of contemplative observation regarding both the higher and the lower.
Just as in the ninth stage, tainted and untainted wholesome states arise mutually as causes for one another;
and just as there is a sequence of taking birth in higher or lower realms,
such as when a mind acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika*) or a resultant mind (*vipākaja*) dies and a defiled state arises.
Seventh, regarding the sequence of essence and function between the lower and upper [realms]:
for example, when a mind of transformation arises from a pure dhyāna,
the mind of transformation successively gives rise to the pure dhyāna and so forth.
Now, based on this principle, I shall clarify the sequential order in which the various mental states arise.
First, we shall discuss the preparatory stage (*prayoga*).
Within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), there is the wholesome mind of the preparatory stage.
Within its own stage, it can produce all [minds],
with the exception of the four dhyāna transformation-minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*) of the desire realm; furthermore,
it can produce the skillful minds of expedient means (*upāya-kuśala-citta*), as well as the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), in the higher stages.
Regarding the cultivation of the generation stage:
from the levels of the desire realm, such as the wisdoms derived from hearing and reflection,
one gives rise to the skillful mind of the preparatory stage for the first dhyāna.

The sequence of contemplative observation proceeds from the wisdoms of hearing and reflection within the desire realm to the wholesome minds of the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) for the first and second dhyānas,
as well as the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Successive attainment:
the skillful mind of the preparatory stage of the first dhyāna ground, as well as the minds of those in training and those beyond training.
Leap-over attainment.
The skillful wholesome minds, the learner’s minds, and the non-learner’s minds arising from the stage of the second dhyāna— among these,
the śrāvaka’s leap-over dhyāna does not exceed one [stage].
Therefore, the same principle applies when comparing all other stages.
As for the bodhisattva,
throughout all stages,
in accordance with whatever mind arises.
All of these can indeed arise.
Why, then, do the innate [attainments] of the higher stages not arise?
All innate attainments [arise].
All [these qualities] follow the retribution of the body;
for when the body resides on a lower stage,
there is no wholesome state acquired by birth belonging to a higher stage.
Why are unwholesome states (*akuśala*) of the higher stages not produced?
Because there are no unwholesome states at all in the higher stages.
Why are obscured (*nivṛta*) states of the higher stages not produced?
When the higher stages disappear and one becomes attached to one's own stage,
one must first complete the skillful means directed toward that [higher stage].
Thereafter, craving arises for what one has acquired for oneself.
For this reason, one does not give rise to defiled thoughts of a higher stage through the preparatory means of a lower stage.
Why does a mind of retribution belonging to a higher stage not arise?
Because when the body is in a lower stage, there is no retribution of a higher stage.
Why does a defiled mind belonging to a higher stage not arise?
Though one is situated in the desire realm and gives rise to the visual, auditory, and other consciousnesses of the first dhyāna,
those consciousnesses that are produced [therein] are [of that same level].
They must rely on the sense organs of the eye, ear, and so forth belonging to a higher stage;
the organs of a higher stage necessarily arise based on the pure meditative concentration (*śuddhadhyāna*) of that higher stage.
Because it does not arise based on the wholesome minds of lower stages.
Why do the *śailpasthānika* (artistic) minds of higher stages not arise?
Because there are no artistic minds in any of the higher stages.
Why is it that the transformation-mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) of a higher stage is not produced?
Because the transformation-mind of a higher stage is the fruit of the pure dhyāna (*śuddhadhyāna*) of that same higher stage.
It is thus in the desire realm.
Within the stages of the form realm, the skillful mind of application [arises] within its own stage.
It can produce all [minds],
with the exception of the transformative minds of the higher dhyānas within its own stage and those belonging to the higher stages.
One gives rise to the wholesome mind of training and the wholesome mind of no-more-training;
in the lower realm of desire,
one gives rise to the wholesome mind of application and the wholesome mind of acquisition.
From unwholesome, defiled, or transformational minds,
there arise, in successive order,
wholesome minds of application and wholesome minds of acquisition.
It is acquired at birth in the desire realm because it is swift;
from the higher stages, it arises sequentially through preparatory effort.
In all other stages, the wholesome minds acquired at birth do not function in this manner;
such is the sequence of their retrogression.
When an unwholesome mind or a defiled mind arises,
the sequence of its activity gives rise to a mind of lower transformation.
Why is it that the minds of retribution-born, deportment, and craftsmanship do not arise within the stages of the desire realm?
Because they are subtle and weak;
they do not arise sequentially from superior wholesome states within their own realm.
Looking toward the lower stages,
one attains five types of mind;
this is the sequence for the successive contemplations.
Having produced the minds of those in training and those beyond training through skillful means,
one subsequently regresses in sequence and produces inferior, defiled states.
The sequence of the arising of function:
the mind that descends to convert beings arises;
it is thus for the realm of form.
Within the formless realm,
the skillful mind of expedient means can produce all [minds] within its own level.
The higher stages are indeterminate;
from the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness,
one can produce the skillful minds of the preparatory stage belonging to the higher realms, as well as the minds of those in training and those beyond training.
In the sphere of nothingness,
one gives rise only to skillful minds of expedient means when looking toward the higher [sphere],
namely, the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Because there is no untainted [state],
neither the mind of training nor the mind beyond training arises.
Since there is nothing further above the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nothing more arises.
One aspires to give rise to four types of minds in the lower stages;
through the sequential process of contemplation,
one gives rise to the preparatory, learner, and non-learner minds.
The sequence of retrogression:
having given rise to the minds of the four formless absorptions (ārūpya-samāpatti), they become obscured and suppressed,
and thus one does not produce emanations (nirmāṇa).
The mind produced through transformation does not arise;
such is the method of skillful means.
Next, the innate [mind] is distinguished.
Within the stages of the desire realm,
the innate wholesome mind [arises] within its own stage.
It can produce all [minds],
with the exception of the mind of transformation,
within the higher stages.
It gives rise only to defilement;
that is to say, because within the desire realm, all defiled states arising from birth and death extend upward to all higher stages.
Why, then, do the preparatory, learner, and non-learner minds of the higher stages not arise there?
Because it is not a skillful means.
Why do the states of birth-attainment, retribution-born, and deportment not arise in the higher stages?
Because their realms and stages are distinct.
Why does one not produce a mind of transformation belonging to a higher stage?
Because a mind of transformation is the fruit of a higher dhyāna, whereas the [minds] acquired at birth in the realm of form belong to their own respective stages.
Within its own level,
there arise the wholesome states produced by effort, those acquired at birth, the defiled, the resultant, and the functional;
with the exception of the mind of transformation and the minds of those in training and those beyond training.
In the higher stages,
only defiled [states] arise;
in the lower stages, [they do not].
One may give rise to unwholesome or defiled minds through birth;
these are acquired at birth within their own respective stages (bhūmi) of the formless realm.
Through the birth of skillful means, one attains a wholesome mind; through the birth of defilement,
one attains a defiled state of existence within the higher realms.
Within the lower stages,
one can give rise to unwholesome and defiled states of mind.
Next, the unwholesome [states] are explained.
One attains an unwholesome mind;
within the desire realm,
it can give rise to all [other states].
Excluding the mind of transformation,
[the mind] does not arise in the higher realms.
Next, the defiled [mind] is explained.
The defiled states of the desire realm are the same as the unwholesome;
the defiled states of the form realm are [unwholesome] within their own level.
The birth-moment consciousness arises as wholesome through application, as defiled, and as pertaining to deportment;
excluding the mind of transformation, the minds of those in training and those beyond training do not arise from it.
In the lower desire realm,
one gives rise to preparatory wholesome states, innate wholesome states, unwholesome states, and defiled states;
this is for the purpose of relying on lower wholesome states to prevent falling back from one's own level.
From the arising of a wholesome mind produced by effort in the desire realm, one acquires a wholesome mind through rebirth; there,
at the end of life in the higher realms,
one undergoes birth in the lower realms with defiled states of existence.
Therefore, one gives rise to unwholesome and defiled states of the desire realm;
from within that same realm, one directs them toward the wholesome states of skillful means and the defiled states of the lower realms. Question:
For what reason can one who is defiled in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) give rise to a wholesome mind acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika-citta*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
whereas a wholesome mind acquired at birth of the same realm does not arise in a lower stage?
The commentary states:
In the desire realm, the wholesome mind acquired at birth is powerful,
sharp, and swift.
It can prevent falling back from the higher [realms];
therefore, it is brought forth.
It is acquired through birth in the higher realms.
Being soft, dull, and unsharp,
it cannot defend against what is above;
therefore, it does not arise.
The formless [minds] that are defiled produce,
within their own stage,
the skillful minds of application, the defiled minds of acquisition, and the minds born of retribution.
In the higher realms, they do not arise;
in the lower realm of desire,
unwholesome minds and defiled minds arise.
This means that because one is reborn in the desire realm after death,
there arise in the lower form realm both skillful minds of preparatory application and defiled minds.
In order to prevent falling back from the higher [realm],
one initiates preparatory means for the lower [realm];
because one dies in the higher [realm] and is born in the lower, one gives rise to a defiled mind.
Regarding the same realm looking down as the form realm does,
some say that the same realm looks down [upon the lower realms].
It merely gives rise to the mind acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika*) and the defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-citta*).
This statement does not appear in the treatise;
it is a mistaken remark by a person.
Next, the resultant minds are distinguished.
Within their own level, the resultant minds of the desire realm [are as follows].
With the exception of the wholesome mind of skillful means and the mind of transformation,
all other [minds] arise,
because they are weak and inferior.
They do not give rise to skillful means,
because their meditative concentration is not pure;
they do not give rise to transformative minds.
In the higher realms,
only defiled states arise;
that is to say, because one who dies there is reborn in a higher realm.
The resultant mind of the form realm can,
within its own stage,
give rise to the defiled minds acquired at birth, as well as the resultant and deportment minds.
In the higher stages,
only defiled states arise;
in the lower stages, both the unwholesome and the defiled can arise.
This is because, upon the end of that life, one is born in a lower realm;
thus, the retributive mind of the formless realm [does not arise] within its own level.
It can give rise to innate defiled states born of retribution;
it produces attachment toward higher realms,
while toward lower realms it produces only unwholesome defilements.
Question: If even unwholesome states can successively give rise to the wholesome mind of skillful means,
why cannot the retributive mind do the same?
The commentary’s own explanation states:
Because the retributive mind is weak and inferior, it does not produce wholesome [states].
Unwholesome [states] and wholesome states do not differ in their objective spheres (*ālambana*).
Because of having seen [the faults],
an unwholesome mind can subsequently give rise to a wholesome mind;
furthermore, the unwholesome mind is a powerful one.
Therefore, one is able to produce wholesome states. Question:
If it is said that a retributive mind, being weak and inferior, does not produce wholesome states, [how can this be so?]
As for why the wholesome mind of skillful means arises there,
the treatise itself explains:
"When the wholesome mind ceases..."
Because he abandons diligent application,
he gives rise to a mind characterized by weak and inferior retribution.
Next, the modes of deportment are distinguished.
The deportment of the desire realm is identical to the retribution of the desire realm;
so too is the deportment of the form realm.
They are the same as the retribution of the form realm.
Next, the craftsmanship is distinguished;
it is the same as the retribution of the deportment in the desire realm.
Question:
Why do the minds of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) not give rise to the wholesome mind of skillful means (*upāya-kuśala-citta*)?
The treatise states:
"These two are produced by their own pleasure;
therefore, they do not give rise to a mind of skillful means."
Why does he not give rise to the minds of those in training or those beyond training? Because they are not skillful means.
Why does he not give rise to the mind of transformation?
Because it is not pure dhyāna,
next the transformative mind is distinguished.
This refers to the transformative mind of the desire realm.
Within its own level,
it produces only the mind of transformation; within the higher levels, [it likewise produces only the mind of transformation].
It is solely the production of skillful means;
that is, entering the fundamental dhyāna from a transformation-mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*).
This refers to the transformation-mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Within its own stage,
only the mind born of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*) and the wholesome mind of skillful means (*upāya-kuśala*) arise from their own respective types.
Therefore, the mind of birth and transformation arises.
Returning from its function to its source,
the mind of skillful means arises.
In the higher realms, one gives rise solely to the wholesome mind of skillful means;
that is, having transformed [the realm] in the second dhyāna, one returns to enter the second dhyāna,
and so on up to the fourth dhyāna, where the same principle applies.
It does not arise from the lower realms.
Next, the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) are distinguished:
the mind of one in training belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Within its own stage,
it produces the skillful minds of both the trainee (*śaikṣa*) and the one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
In the higher stages, it produces only the skillful mind of expedient means and the mind of the trainee.
For what reason does one not give rise to the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) in the higher stages?
Because the state of no-more-learning in the higher stages necessarily arises based upon the pure dhyāna (śuddha-dhyāna) of those higher stages.
In the lower Desire Realm,
one gives rise to the wholesome mind of application and the wholesome mind of acquisition;
from the perspective of the same realm looking down, [these arise].
Regarding the arising of the wholesome [states] acquired through application (*prayoga-pratilambhika*) and the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa-citta*):
for what reason do those acquired by birth (*upapatti-lābhika*) not arise?
As it is stated in the commentary on the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*:
Because it is acquired at birth in the desire realm and is both powerful and swift,
it arises in immediate succession from a mind of training (śaikṣa).
That which is acquired through birth in the higher realms is weak and not sharp; therefore,
it follows after the mind of training.
It cannot be produced.
For what reason is it that the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) is not produced? It is because the state of no-more-learning of a lower stage [is not produced].
Because it must arise based on the pure dhyānas of the lower stages,
the learner's mind of the formless realm is the same as that of the form realm.
Excluding the desire realm,
it is distant from the form of the desire realm because one is not reborn there.
Next, the Aśaikṣas of the form realm are distinguished within their own stage.
One gives rise to the wholesome mind of skillful means and the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
For what reason does one not give rise to the mind of one in training (śaikṣa) at the time of attaining the state beyond training?
Because of the relinquishing of the mind of training (*śaikṣa*),
when one falls away from the state of no-more-training (*aśaikṣa*),
it is the defiled mind that falls away, not the mind of training.
The mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-citta) does not give rise to the mind of one in training (śaikṣa-citta).
Within the higher stages,
it gives rise to the wholesome minds of skillful means (upāya-kuśala) and the mind of one beyond training.
This refers to the Arhat’s sporting through the various stages (bhūmi),
whether arising from the untainted (anāsrava) mind to a tainted (sāsrava) mind,
or arising from a tainted mind to an untainted one.
In the lower realm of desire,
there arise both the wholesome states acquired through effort (*prayoga-prāpta-kuśala*) and those acquired by birth (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*);
this is also because the wholesome states acquired by birth in the desire realm are powerful and sharp.
Upon being born, one acquires the wholesome minds of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) and the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), belonging to the same realm and a lower stage.
It is not produced in the higher realms because it is not strong or sharp; therefore,
it does not arise there.
The formless [attainments] and the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) also give rise to the preparatory mind and the mind of one beyond training within their own respective stages.
The same applies to those above and below;
the sequence is thus.
Within the context of what is produced,
one isolates the principle of the six sense objects giving rise to consciousness and takes this as the "object-condition" (ālambana-pratyaya).
It takes on the sense of producing consciousness within the six faculties,
and it acts as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for all other phenomena without obstruction.
The essential characteristics are thus.
This concludes the two sections [of the preceding].
Next, we shall analyze and determine their conditions (*pratyaya*) with respect to all phenomena (*dharma*).
If mental factors arise,
they depend upon four conditions;
mental factors must necessarily possess associated and co-existent [factors].
Such matters as these constitute causes and conditions;
the mind relies upon its prior births.
This is the condition as immediate antecedent (samanantara-pratyaya).
The mind arises depending upon objects;
this is its condition as object (ālambana-pratyaya).
The mind arises dependent upon the faculties;
these are its predominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
This is according to the Abhidharma.
The attainment of non-perception and the attainment of cessation arise from three conditions;
so it is proclaimed in that school.
The cessation of non-conception is a conditioned phenomenon;
it possesses arising, abiding, and ceasing simultaneously and coexistently.
Mutual assistance is its causal condition;
it arises based on the preceding mind.
This is the condition as immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
That all phenomena do not obstruct one another is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Because they are not mental phenomena (citta-dharma),
they lack an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
This applies to all other non-mental phenomena as well.
All are produced by two conditions,
namely the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*),
including all factors that are of one's own category and those shared with others.
This is its causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
That all phenomena do not obstruct it is its dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Because it does not arise through the guidance of a preceding mind,
it lacks an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*);
since it is not a mental state (*citta-dharma*), it is incapable of taking an object as its cognitive domain.
There is no object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Thus, the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* says:
"The mind and all mental factors..."
These arise from four conditions;
the two meditative attainments arise from three;
as for the rest, it is said they arise from two.
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi*,
only the mind and mental factors arise from four conditions.
All other phenomena that are not of the nature of mind arise from only two conditions;
none of them possess the status of being either an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) or an object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Therefore, that treatise states:
"The object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) of the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) consists of mind and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma)."
Because it was previously opened and guided by that [text], there is a sequential order.
Because it arises through the apprehension and grasping of those six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), there is an object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
This is stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
The explanation is the same for this as well;
thus, that text states:
"The mind and mental factors continue in an uninterrupted succession."
It is called the sequential condition because the mind and mental factors arise by taking objects as their conditions.
It is called the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
According to this text,
it is the sequential object-condition (*samanantara-ālambana-pratyaya*).
The dharmas that arise from the sphere produce mind;
those that do not belong to the sphere do not produce mind.
Someone has explained this as follows:
Phenomena that are not of the nature of mind also depend upon conditions;
however, there is no textual authority for this in the sūtras or śāstras.
This is merely human speech;
these words are erroneous and frivolous,
and it is not appropriate to accept them hastily.
These three sections are concluded.
Next, we shall distinguish their similarities and differences by comparing the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
As for the characteristics of these similarities and differences:
As stated in the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra:
that which is called "identical" refers to the names and meanings of the four conditions (*catvāraḥ pratyayāḥ*).
It is the same as the Abhidharma;
the point of difference is that within the teachings of the Hīnayāna, [it is stated as follows].
Following these characteristics,
it is said that the Bodhisattva understands them to be like illusions or like the moon reflected in water;
they have no fixed nature, yet their illusory appearances are not non-existent.
Therefore, that text states:
"Just as the moon in water can be seen with the eyes but cannot be grasped by the hand,
so too is the destruction [of phenomena] by the Sage."
One can shatter the moon that can be grasped,
but one cannot shatter that which is visible;
the four conditions are likewise so.
The characteristics exist as entities yet lack substantiality,
and thus cannot be definitively grasped;
for this reason, it differs from the two vehicles.

The meaning of the four conditions has been briefly explained in this manner. 19. The Meaning of the Five Fruits (Three Editions). The meaning of the five fruits is analyzed through ten gates: listing their names and defining their characteristics; (1) analysis in relation to the six causes; (2) analysis in relation to the ten causes; (3) analysis in relation to the four conditions; (4) analysis in relation to the outflowing and non-outflowing; (5) analysis in relation to the three natures; (6) analysis in relation to the three periods of time; (7) analysis in relation to the various stages (*bhūmi*); (8) analysis in relation to those in training and so forth; (9) analysis in relation to the dharmas to be abandoned; (10) [the tenth gate]. Within the first gate:
The enumeration of names and the discernment of characteristics regarding the meaning of the five fruits are set forth in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*.
In the Abhidharma-śāstra,
this is also analyzed in detail:
that which recompenses a cause is called a fruit.
The fruits are distinct and not identical;
they are explained as five within a single category.
What are these five names?
First is the fruit of retribution;
second is the fruit of dependence;
third is the fruit of human effort.
In the Abhidharma-śāstra,
these are termed the fruit of effort and the four fruits of predominance.
The five fruits of liberation.
Regarding what is called the fruit of retribution:
it refers to wholesome and unwholesome karma.
Obtaining the retribution of suffering or pleasure is called the fruit of retribution (*vipākaphala*).
As for the term "fruit of outflow" (*niṣyandaphala*):
From the good arises the good;
from the evil arises the evil.
Such is the nature of all phenomena that are of the same kind.
Because it arises subsequently based on what preceded it,
it is called the "fruit of reliance" (niṣyanda-phala).
As for the "fruit of human effort" (puruṣakāra-phala):
As stated in the *Bhūmivastu*:
divination, seals, arithmetic, and the administration of official affairs—
all such things as these.
Each has its own fruit that arises;
this is called the "fruit of the person" (puruṣakāraphala).
"Person" (puruṣa) refers to a human being.
That which is produced by a person is called the fruit of the person.
As for the fruit of effort:
As stated in the Abhidharma,
that which is obtained through effort and power is called the fruit of application (*prayoga-phala*).
Although these two statements differ in wording,
their meaning is not distinct.
As for the "predominant fruit" (adhipatiphala):
As stated in the *Bhūmivastu*,
the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*) are called "predominant" (*adhipati*).
Each has its own fruit that arises,
which is called the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
For example, the eye gives rise to visual consciousness.
In all such cases,
according to the Abhidharma,
when a single dharma arises:
All phenomena of the past and present do not obstruct this;
they are all termed "predominant" (adhipati).
Regarding the dharmas that arise, they are called "dominant fruits" (adhipatiphala) in relation to those [causes];
this definition is thus universal and applies not only to the twenty-two faculties (indriya).
Regarding the fruit of liberation:
according to the Abhidharma,
it consists of the untainted noble path (anāsrava-āryamārga) and its corresponding knowledge (sāmānya-jñāna).
The extinction of all afflictions is called the fruit of liberation.
If one relies on the *Dharmaskandhapāda-śāstra*, it is as follows:
The untainted noble path,
which eternally severs the afflictions,
is called the fruit of liberation.
The conventional knowledge and so forth that extinguish all afflictions are not ultimate.
This concludes the single section on that which is not the fruit of liberation.
Next, the five fruits are distinguished in relation to the six causes.
As for the "six causes":
Namely, the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu),
the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu),
and the associated cause (saṃprayuktaka-hetu).
The common cause,
the pervasive cause,
and the retributive cause.
As for the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*):
when anything arises, the fact that all phenomena do not obstruct it is called the efficient cause.
Regarding self-causation:
all conditioned phenomena arise from their own kind.
That which is called the self-nature cause (svabhāva-hetu). As for the associated cause (samprayuktaka-hetu),
it consists of all minds and mental factors (citta-caitta).
Existing at the same time,
they act as corresponding conditions for one another,
relying upon each other.
That which possesses functional activity is called the associated cause (saṃprayuktaka-hetu).
As for the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu):
Among conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*),
those factors that exist simultaneously are termed "coexistent" (*sahabhū*).
The principle of coexistence is that things stand in mutual dependence;
this is termed the "coexistent cause" (sahabhū-hetu).
The aforementioned associated cause (samprayuktaka-hetu) applies exclusively to mental factors (caitta),
for they rely upon one another and function in mutual dependence.
This common cause (sādhāraṇa-hetu) pervades all three aggregates;
its nature is established through mutual causality.
There is this distinction.
Regarding the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*):
under the Truths of Suffering and its Origin, views, doubt, and ignorance universally enable the increase of all outflows (*āsrava*).
It is called the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
As for the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*),
it refers to wholesome and unwholesome karma.
Because it can produce suffering and pleasure,
it is called the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
This meaning is explained in detail in the chapter on the six causes.
Question:
By what cause can one obtain what fruit? Answer:
What is performed attains the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) and the fruit of liberation (*vimuktiphala*).
Specifically, it corresponds to these;
generally, it also attains the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*).
Because it is taught that the three conditions function as the "produced" (kārya),
the meaning is as explained below. [This refers to] the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) and the pervasive cause (sarvatraga-hetu).
It can obtain the fruit of reliance (niśraya-phala);
it obtains the fruit of application (puruṣakāra-phala) through association (samprayukta) and coexistence (sahabhū).
Regarding the single type of retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*), it is able to obtain the fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*); these two sections are concluded.
Next, the five fruits are explained in relation to the ten causes.
This meaning has been fully and extensively analyzed in the subsequent chapter on the ten causes; thus concludes the analysis of these three gateways.
Next, the five fruits are distinguished in relation to the four conditions (*catvāraḥ pratyayāḥ*).
Regarding the "four conditions":
As previously stated, among the six causes, these include the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*),
the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
These five kinds are explained as causes and conditions.
Regarding the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*):
They are taught as three conditions:
namely, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Among the four conditions, [these three are included].
A single type of causal condition can produce three kinds of results: namely,
the retributive result (*vipākaphala*), the dominant result (*adhipatiphala*), and the result of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*).
Among these, the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is able to produce its own retributive fruit (*vipāka-phala*),
while the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) produces its own [homogeneous] fruit.
One is able to obtain the fruit of reliance (*niśraya-phala*),
which consists of the associated (*samprayukta*) and co-existent (*sahabhū*) factors;
one obtains the fruit of effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
The remaining three conditions can each produce three fruits.
As for the condition as immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*):
It obtains the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
It takes one kind of object as its objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
It obtains the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Regarding the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*):
it yields the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) and the fruit of liberation (*vimukti-phala*). These four sections are concluded.
Next, the five fruits are explained by contrasting them with causes that are either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
There are three types of outflowing (sāsrava) phenomena:
first, the wholesome; second, the unwholesome; and third, the indeterminate.
The wholesome are of two kinds.
First, the wholesome state that severs the fetters,
namely the mundane path of non-obstruction.
Second, the state that does not sever the fetters.
This refers to all wholesome dharmas of the desire realm,
as well as all wholesome dharmas of liberation, excellence, and progress within the eight dhyānas;
these are the wholesome [dharmas] that sever the fetters.
Regarding the number of fruits attained,
the treatises offer differing explanations.
If one follows the Abhidharma:
One is able to attain the five fruits;
by means of these wholesome dharmas,
one is able to obtain a favorable retribution.
Therefore, there is the fruit of retribution (*vipākaphala*).
Because [dharmas] arise from those of the same kind, there is the fruit of dependence (*niṣyandaphala*).
[This occurs] simultaneously.
The middle [category] consists of those that correspond and coexist,
mutually supporting one another to produce a fruit through effortful application.
It does not obstruct the myriad dharmas and possesses a sovereign fruit (adhipatiphala),
because it severs the fetters.
There is the fruit of liberation.
If based on the *Dharmaskandha*,
one attains only four fruits.
Excluding the fruit of liberation,
mundane abandonment of the fetters is not liberation.
One who has not severed the fetters can attain the four fruits,
excluding the fruit of liberation.
It is thus with wholesome dharmas.
As for unwholesome dharmas,
they likewise yield four fruits.
As for indeterminate dharmas,
they can obtain three fruits,
excluding the fruit of liberation and the fruit of retribution.
There are three other types.
Thus it is with the contaminated (*sāsrava*).
Regarding the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas:
There are two kinds: first,
the untainted state that severs the fetters,
namely the unimpeded path of both seeing and cultivation.
Second is the non-abandonment of fetters,
which refers to all untainted wholesome dharmas of liberation and further progress;
it is the untainted state that abandons the fetters.
One can attain the four fruits [of the spiritual path],
excluding the fruit of retribution,
because uncontaminated dharmas do not produce retributive results.
One who has not severed the fetters can attain three fruits—
excluding the fruit of liberation and the retributive fruit. This concludes the five gates.
Next, the five fruits are distinguished according to the three natures.
Regarding virtuous karma,
it likewise employs virtuous dharmas.
These are considered the four fruits;
the fruit of retribution is excluded because the wholesome is not retribution.
Unwholesome dharmas function as two kinds of results, namely:
the result of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the dominant result (*adhipati-phala*).
From a preceding wholesome state of mind,
a subsequent unwholesome state arises;
this is sequential dependent origination.
This is called the fruit of effort;
it takes the preceding wholesome mind as its mental faculty (manas-indriya).
The arising of unwholesome consciousness through a predominant condition is called the predominant fruit (adhipatiphala).
Because unwholesome dharmas are not retribution,
they lack a fruit of retribution;
nor are they dharmas that arise through the production of their own kind.
There is no fruit of reliance,
because it is not liberation;
there is no fruit of liberation.
Using indeterminate dharmas as three fruits,
excluding their fruit of support (*niśraya-phala*).
Because they are not of the same category,
they are not the fruit of liberation;
for indeterminate dharmas are not liberation.
As for unwholesome karma,
it likewise takes the unwholesome as its three fruits.
Excluding the fruit of retribution and the fruit of liberation,
those wholesome dharmas are taken as the two fruits.
This refers to the fruit of effort and the sovereign fruit;
that is, the arising of subsequent wholesome dharmas from preceding unwholesome ones.
The sequential dependent origination is called the fruit of effort;
it follows from a preceding unwholesome mind.
It takes the mind-faculty (manas) as the basis for the arising of subsequent wholesome states of mind,
and it constitutes the mental consciousness (manovijñāna).
That which arises from the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) is called the dominant fruit (adhipati-phala).
Because it is wholesome and not a retribution,
it lacks a retribution fruit (vipāka-phala).
Because they are not of the same category,
there is no fruit of reliance for those unwholesome dharmas.
Because the fetters are not severed,
there is no fruit of liberation;
this is due to the use of indeterminate dharmas.
These are considered the four fruits, excluding the fruit of liberation.
Question: Why?
Unwholesome states and indeterminate states are not of the same class.
For what reason?
It can have a fruit of dependence (*niśraya-phala*).
The treatise itself explains:
"Within the stages of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)."
Although this is indeterminate,
it is similar in kind to the defiled unwholesome afflictions of that desire realm;
because they are of the same class.
From those unwholesome states, this indeterminate state arises;
it is termed an "adhipati-phala" (dominant fruit).
Furthermore, there are the views, doubt, and ignorance belonging to the realms of suffering and its origin.
This is its pervasive cause;
this pervasive cause increases all defiled phenomena.
Within the stages of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the two views— the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)—
are called "dependent fruits" because they arise based on these causes;
[they are produced by] indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) karma.
Furthermore, the indeterminate (avyākṛta) is taken as three fruits:
namely, the fruit of reliance (niśraya-phala), the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala), and the dominant fruit (adhipati-phala).
This is because indeterminate karma is not a cause of retribution (vipāka-hetu).
It lacks its retributive fruit,
because being indeterminate (avyākṛta), it is not a dharma of liberation; thus,
it lacks the fruit of liberation.
Those wholesome dharmas serve as two kinds of fruits,
namely the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*),
arising from the preceding neutral state.
The subsequent arising of goodness through sequential dependent origination is called the fruit of effort.
An indeterminate mind serves as the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) that gives rise to subsequent wholesome minds.
It is considered the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Because it arises through the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) and is wholesome rather than a result of maturation (*vipāka*), it is called the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
There is no ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*),
because it is not of the same category.
There is no dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
As for indeterminate dharmas,
because they do not sever the fetters,
there is no fruit of liberation.
Unwholesome dharmas are taken as three fruits,
excluding the fruit of retribution and the fruit of liberation.
Question: For what reason can there be an adhipati-phala (dominant fruit)?
This principle is the same as the previous principle concerning how unwholesome karma relates to the arising of an adhipati-phala from neutral dharmas.
The predominance of functional efficacy can be understood by analogy with what precedes; this concludes the six gates.
Next, their characteristics are distinguished according to the three periods of time.
Past karma, when compared with the dharmas of the three periods of time,
can have four kinds of results.
Excluding the fruit of liberation,
because the dharma of liberation does not fall within the world;
[this refers to] present dharmas.
Regarding the present dharmas,
two fruits can be obtained:
namely, the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala) and the sovereign fruit (adhipati-phala).
Because it lacks anteriority and posteriority,
it has neither retributive fruit nor dominant fruit;
it has no fruit of liberation.
The meaning is the same as explained previously. Question:
In the present, one still looks toward the present; there is no sequence of before and after.
Therefore, regarding those [karmas] that have no subsequent retributive fruit (*vipākaphala*) or dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*),
how could they exist if they have already passed away into the past?
The commentary states:
Looking back from the past to the past,
because the duration of time is vast and long, it is possible for this to exist.
The present is observed within the present;
because its duration is extremely brief, it does not [persist].
Looking from the present toward the future,
there are still four fruits,
excluding the fruit of liberation.
Future karma, in relation to future dharmas,
can obtain three fruits.
That which is called the fruit of retribution (*vipākaphala*) consists of the predominance of functional effort (*prayoga-adhipati*);
it lacks the fruit of reliance (*niśrayaphala*) and the fruit of liberation (*vimuktiphala*).
The meaning of the absence of the fruit of liberation is to be understood as follows.
For what reason is there no fruit of reliance?
Because that which is future has not yet arisen.
Because there is no before or after.
If this is so, why can there be a retributive fruit?
The explanation states:
There are cases where a fruit arises from a retributive cause through the mutual arising of different categories;
although the phenomenon exists in the future,
the characteristics of cause and effect are already differentiated.
Therefore, it is said that they exist.
If one discusses their fruit of dependence,
they arise from causes of the same kind.
Since they are of the same kind and difficult to distinguish,
one must refer to the place where they have already arisen in order to speak of their fruit of support (*niśraya-phala*).
In future time,
both cause and effect are equally yet to arise.
Because it is difficult to distinguish between its preceding and succeeding moments,
there is no fruit of reliance (*niśraya-phala*).
If that is so, why are there the fruit of effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*)?
The predominance of functional activity cannot be established as either preceding or succeeding,
yet it does exist; thus concludes the section on these seven gates.
Next, the five fruits are distinguished according to the various stages (*bhūmi*).
"Stages" refers to the nine stages,
ranging from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
How are the fruits obtained?
As stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*:
"In each respective stage, there are four [paths] of that same stage."
Alternatively, there are two [liberations] belonging to other stages;
if one correctly contemplates those stages,
there is likewise the fruit of liberation.
Regarding the initial statement that "within one's own stage, there are four [results] for one's own stage":
this means that an action belonging to its own stage can obtain four results in relation to the phenomena of its own stage.
Excluding the fruit of liberation,
as for what was said regarding "either [karma] of another stage," this refers to karma that is with outflows (sāsrava).
Looking back toward the tainted dharmas of other stages,
two fruits can be obtained:
namely, the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
After a mind of its own level, a mind of another level arises;
this is an immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya) and has the fruit of effortful application.
The mind of its own stage serves as the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) that gives rise to consciousness of another stage.
It arises from a dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) and has a dominant fruit (adhipati-phala),
provided it is uncontaminated karma (anāsrava-karma).
One aspires to the untainted dharmas within other stages;
because the resulting fruits obtained therein— whether they have a basis or not—
are indeterminate in quantity, it is said that they are "either."
Question:
For what reason are the contaminated dharmas,
when compared to those of other stages, [not considered superior]?
The fruit of dependence (*niśraya-phala*) is not mentioned when comparing uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) states with one another;
is the fruit of dependence then mentioned?
The commentary states:
Because they are bound by different levels (bhūmi),
when compared across different levels, [they are distinct].
The categories and names differ;
therefore, it is not a fruit of reliance.
Furthermore, untainted phenomena are not dharmas bound to a specific stage.
Therefore, when different stages are compared with one another,
it can be said that they possess the fruit of reliance (*niśraya-phala*).
If one correctly contemplates the stage, there is also the fruit of liberation (*vimukti-phala*).
It should be known that this refers to the eight stages of dhyāna and the path of non-obstruction.
Furthermore, there is its fruit of liberation; this concludes the eight gates.
Next, we shall distinguish the five fruits with respect to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and others.
There are three kinds of phenomena (*dharma*).
First, the dharmas of training;
second, the dharmas beyond training;
third, the dharmas that are neither of training nor beyond training.
In the study of the acquisition of learning, there are three kinds of fruits:
namely, the fruit of reliance (*niṣyanda-phala*), the fruit of effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), and the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Because they arise from similar types, they are called the fruit of reliance.
It is associated and co-existent;
furthermore, as a sequential condition, it has a result produced through effort,
wherein the preceding [moment] serves as the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*).
Subsequently, it becomes the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
It arises through the condition of predominance (*adhipatipratyaya*) and possesses the fruit of predominance (*adhipatiphala*).
The dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣadharma) also constitute three fruits;
they are similar to the previous case.
Using those dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner as three fruits:
namely, the fruit of liberation (vimukti-phala),
the fruit of effort (puruṣakāra-phala), and the dominant fruit (adhipati-phala).
Unconditioned liberation is neither the mind of one in training nor the mind of one beyond training; therefore,
there exists the fruit of liberation.
When a contaminated mind arises subsequent to a mind that has been cultivated,
its arising as an immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) is called the fruit of effort (puruṣakāra-phala).
Using that mind of training as the mental faculty (manas-indriya),
one gives rise to a mind associated with outflows (sāsrava-citta).
It is considered the mental consciousness;
that which arises through the dominant condition is called the dominant fruit.
Regarding the karma of one beyond training:
it takes the dharmas of one beyond training as its three fruits.
That is to say: the fruit of reliance, the fruit of human effort, and the sovereign fruit;
taking those factors of training as one single fruit.
This refers to the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
That is to say, when one who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) subsequently regresses and gives rise to a mind of training (*śaikṣa*),
the state of being beyond training does not act as an obstacle to that [regression].
There is a superior fruit. Question:
Why is there no fruit of reliance?
A superior dharma does not depend upon an inferior one as its cause.
Furthermore, he asked:
Why is it that the fruit of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*) is not a dharma that is associated (*samprayukta*) or co-existent (*sahabhū*)?
Furthermore, because it is not a dharma that arises through successive production (*kramotpāda*).
Question: It was stated previously that after the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣacitta), there arises a regressive mind of one in training (śaikṣacitta).
Why, then, do you say that this is not a sequential [arising]?
The commentary states:
Although one who has attained the state beyond training may later regress and give rise to a mind of training,
within that state beyond training...
There is ultimately no principle of regression;
it is only when one remains within the realm of outflows (sāsrava) that the possibility of regression exists.
Therefore, it is not sequential.
Because it is not sequential,
there is no fruit of effortful application.
Using those dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner as two fruits,
namely: the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
After a mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣacitta), a conventional mind (laukikacitta) arises;
it is a sequential condition (samanantarapratyaya) and possesses the fruit of effortful application (sābhisaṃskāraphala).
The faculty of mind of one beyond training gives rise to a conventional mind,
which constitutes mental consciousness.
That which arises from a dominant condition is called the dominant fruit.
This applies if that karma is neither that of one in training nor that of one beyond training.
Furthermore, one takes dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner as the five fruits; likewise,
one takes those learner-dharmas and non-learner-dharmas [as the five fruits].
There are also two fruits, namely the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*). This concludes the nine gates.
Next, the five fruits are distinguished according to the dharmas that are abandoned.
There are three kinds of dharmas.
The first is that which is abandoned through vision;
this refers to the afflictions of the vision of the truths.
The second is abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahāṇa*).
This refers to the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga-kleśa*), as well as all contaminated karma and its results.
Regarding the afflictions of the path of cultivation:
The essence of right abandonment itself severs the remaining karmic fruits;
it merely cuts the fetters.
Its substance is not interrupted;
the third is "uninterrupted," referring to untainted (anāsrava) dharmas and karma.
Karma to be abandoned by insight takes those dharmas abandoned by insight as its three fruits.
Excluding those fruits of retribution and the fruit of liberation,
one takes the dharmas abandoned through cultivation as the four fruits.
Excluding the fruit of liberation,
one takes the uninterrupted dharmas as a single fruit.
This refers to the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*);
because karma to be abandoned by insight cannot obstruct those [factors]— namely, the abandonment of fetters through wisdom and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
There is a dominant fruit (adhipati-phala) for karma to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya),
which employs the factors to be abandoned by cultivation.
These are considered the four fruits;
excluding the fruit of liberation,
they are attained by means of dharmas abandoned through vision.
These are considered two fruits:
namely, the fruit of effort (*puruṣakāraphala*),
because they arise in succession.
And as for the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*),
it acts as the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) because it gives rise to those phenomena.
The uninterrupted dharmas function as three fruits: namely,
the fruit of liberation and the predominant fruit.
By relying on mundane dhyāna,
one eliminates afflictions and thereby attains the fruit of liberation.
Because one gives rise to the untainted (anāsrava) based on mundane dhyāna,
one attains the fruit of effort and the sovereign fruit (adhipatiphala).
Karma that is uninterrupted takes the uninterrupted dharmas as its four fruits.
Excluding its retributive fruit,
one takes the factors abandoned through seeing as a single fruit.
This refers to the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
Since this fruit is broad and pervasive,
it can be said to exist [in this case].
One employs the methods of cultivation and abandonment as two kinds of fruits:
namely, the fruit of effort and the dominant fruit.
After an untainted mind (anāsrava-citta), a tainted mind (sāsrava-citta) arises;
because it is produced through the condition of immediate succession (samanantara-pratyaya),
it is a fruit of effort (prayoga-phala).
The untainted mental faculty (anāsrava-manas) gives rise to tainted consciousness (sāsrava-vijñāna),
being activated by way of the predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
Therefore, there is the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
Thus has the meaning of the five fruits been briefly explained.

20. The Meaning of the Six Causes (Three Editions): A Fivefold Analysis to Discern Their Characteristics. I. Analysis according to time; II. Analysis in relation to the fruit; III. Analysis traversing the dharmas; IV. Analysis of similarities and differences between the Great and Small Vehicles. First, the characteristics are explained.
The meaning of the six causes is set forth in the Abhidharma-śāstra and the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra.
It is also extensively analyzed into two types:
first, the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu);
second, the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu).
Third, the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu);
fourth, the pervasive cause (sarvatraga-hetu);
fifth, the associated cause (samprayuktaka-hetu).
The sixth is the cause of retribution (*vipāka-hetu*).
Thus, that verse says:
"That which is performed, together with its own class (*sabhāga*), all that is associated is retribution."
From these six kinds of causes,
conditioned phenomena arise.
As for the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu):
When any phenomena arise,
with the exception of their own intrinsic nature,
the myriad dharmas do not obstruct one another.
That which causes something to arise is called the efficient cause (kāraṇahetu),
such as space causing the arising of form.
It is like the earth giving rise to grasses, trees, and so forth.
Therefore, that verse says:
"The similar and the dissimilar."
Excluding its own self-nature,
everything is a productive cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*),
because it does not obstruct at the time of arising.
Regarding the common cause (sabhāga-hetu):
